description: We are a multidisciplinary team of three Computer Scientists, one Computer Engineer, one Mechanical Engineer, and one Mechatronics Engineer. Our expertise spans software development, AI and machine learning, data analysis, IoT, and hardware-software integration. We combine our different engineering and computing backgrounds to turn complex data into practical decision-support solutions.
summary:
Gaiapus connects NASA Earth observations with crop decisions and a practical path to local sensing. Built for Field Shift, our multilingual app combines NASA POWER weather, including IMERG rainfall, with crop calendars and soil assumptions in a reproducible FAO-56 water balance. Maps, 3D views and rainfall scenarios make soil-cover and water trade-offs visible.

Our custom hardware design pairs a solar-powered ESP32-S3 controller with a protected capacitive probe for soil moisture and temperature at 15 and 40 cm, plus air temperature, humidity and local rainfall. LoRa links stakes to a shared gateway, avoiding cellular connections at each sensor. A rechargeable LiFePO4 battery, deep sleep, buffered readings and on-demand LEDs support the goal of affordable monitoring in remote fields. We developed PCB and enclosure designs and tested firmware logic in simulation; field calibration and live app integration remain next steps.

In our six-season historical simulation for Sorriso, Brazil, adding brachiaria to soybean-maize provides about 115 extra crop-cover days annually, with nearly unchanged average water reserves before the next soybean planting. These results depend on stated assumptions.

Gaiapus makes sources, limitations and alternatives visible so farmers and agronomists can assess adaptation choices together.
details:
Repository: https://github.com/LuksbellN/Gaiapus-APP


Gaiapus helps farmers and agronomists compare crop choices, soil cover and water availability. Built for Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data, our web application combines Earth observations, daily simulations and interactive visualizations. Users select a location, check available evidence and compare scenarios through maps, 3D views and technical reports. The interface supports Portuguese, English, Spanish, French and German on desktop and mobile.


Gaiapus planning interface: illustrative soybean development, daily water balance and scenario indicators linked to the selected simulation.

NASA POWER supplies meteorological inputs, GPM IMERG provides rainfall, and Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 imagery supports RGB and NDVI views in demonstration areas. IBGE agricultural statistics, USDA NASS records and INMET station observations support yield research and rainfall evaluation. We preserve source provenance, geographic scale and limitations.

Our deterministic FAO-56 water-balance model combines weather and stage-dependent crop coefficients to track soil-water storage, evapotranspiration, drainage and water deficit. Future-planning scenarios replay historical weather trajectories to explore seasonal variability, rather than predict weather on specific dates. The 3D scenes illustrate modeled crop stages and soil conditions.

In Sorriso, Brazil, we compared three strategies over six historical seasons (2015/2016–2020/2021): soybean-maize-fallow, soybean-maize with brachiaria cover, and soybean followed by long fallow. Under the same weather and a 55 mm available-soil-water assumption, brachiaria added approximately 115 days per year with a crop or cover present, while average reserves before the next soybean planting remained nearly unchanged. Rainfall sensitivity tests use 80%, 100% and 120% of the historical sequence. These are modeled calendar and water outcomes; yield, profit, erosion and carbon benefits were not measured.

Historical Sorriso comparison, averaged over six seasons. Brachiaria adds approximately 115 crop or cover days, while modeled reserves before soybean planting remain similar under the stated assumptions.

Separate machine-learning research compares Ridge regression, gradient boosting and neural networks against historical yield baselines, with temporal and geographic separation during evaluation. In our retrospective test for 2022–2024 across 790 Brazilian municipalities, the selected soybean model reduced mean absolute error from approximately 714 to 582 kg/ha. We also document experiments that did not outperform their baselines. Yield-estimation accuracy does not establish the benefits of changing management.

The application uses React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre and Three.js/React Three Fiber, with a Node.js/Fastify API and Python scientific services. scikit-learn and PyTorch support model research. Docker containers run on Microsoft Azure; Supabase provides authentication and PostgreSQL storage. Technical reports use deterministic templates linked to simulation artifacts, preserving results across languages. Claude and Codex assisted code, tests, documentation and translation under team review.

Our hardware design provides a path toward local sensing: a solar-powered ESP32-S3 stake with soil moisture and temperature sensing at 15 and 40 cm, air temperature, humidity and rainfall. LoRa links stakes to a shared Wi-Fi/MQTT gateway to reduce connectivity requirements. We developed KiCad PCB designs, mechanical CAD and C/C++ firmware with PlatformIO/Arduino. Custom-board manufacturing, calibration, physical validation and secure telemetry integration remain pending; the application's sensor workflow uses explicitly labeled synthetic readings.

CAD render of the Gaiapus controller and rain-gauge assembly. Manufacturing, calibration and live telemetry validation remain pending.

Gaiapus connects regional observations, transparent simulations and local-sensing design in one accessible workflow. We considered missing data, publication delays, uncertainty, privacy, mobile usability, energy, connectivity and cost. Our intended impact is better-informed adaptation decisions with agronomists. Calibrated hardware and supervised field trials are the next steps toward evaluating practical water, yield and financial benefits.
